opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a really natural complementarity there. For decades, the hard part of formal verification hasn't been the checking. Once you have a proof, checking it is mechanical, and tools like theorem provers and SMT solvers are extremely good at that. The hard part has been *finding* the proof: coming up with the right loop invariants, the right lemmas, the right decomposition of the problem, and writing the specification in the first place. That's historically required a lot of very specialized human expertise. It's one of the reasons formal methods have been seen as expensive and hard to scale beyond a relatively small community.

Generative AI is good at exactly that kind of creative, heuristic guessing. It's seen an enormous amount of code and mathematics, so it can propose an invariant or a proof step that's often plausible. But on its own it can be wrong. It hallucinates. So what you get is a very nice pairing: the language model proposes, and the automated reasoning tool disposes. The model generates candidate proofs or specifications, and the prover either confirms them with mathematical certainty or comes back with a counterexample that you can feed back into the model to try again. You keep the soundness guarantees of formal reasoning, but you get a lot of help with the search.

The other side of it, which I find really exciting, is the specification problem. A lot of what blocks people is translating what they actually mean, often written in natural language, policies or documentation or requirements, into formal logic. LLMs are surprisingly good at helping with that translation, and you can then use reasoning tools to check the result for consistency, ask questions back to the user, and find ambiguities. That opens verification up to a much broader set of people who aren't logicians.

And it goes in both directions. As more and more code gets written by generative AI, we need a way to trust that code. Automated reasoning gives you that. So I see the two as reinforcing each other: generative AI makes verification more accessible and scalable, and verification makes generative AI more trustworthy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the thing to understand about program verification is that it's really a search problem, and it's a search problem where checking a candidate answer is cheap and finding the candidate is hard. If I want to prove a loop terminates, or that some piece of code never dereferences a null pointer, or that an access control policy never lets the wrong principal in, what I ultimately need is a proof. And the proof usually hinges on some creative artifact: a loop invariant, a ranking function, an inductive hypothesis, the right abstraction of the heap. Once you have that artifact, a very mechanical and very trustworthy checker can confirm it's correct. The expensive part, the part that has kept formal methods from scaling, is coming up with the artifact in the first place.

For decades we've attacked that with clever heuristics. Abstract interpretation, counterexample-guided refinement, interpolation, all of these are really strategies for guessing invariants well. They work, and we've shipped them at scale in products at AWS. But they hit walls, and when they hit walls a human expert has to step in and supply the insight.

What large language models give us is a new and surprisingly good guesser. They've read an enormous amount of code and an enormous amount of mathematics, and they have decent intuition about what the "shape" of an invariant should be for a given program. And here's the key point: I don't have to trust them. The model proposes, and Lean or Dafny or an SMT solver disposes. If the model hallucinates an invariant, the checker rejects it, we feed the failure back, and it tries again. That loop is exactly the structure where generative AI is safe to use, because the soundness lives in the checker, not in the model.

There are a couple of other things that excite me. One is specification. Historically, the biggest barrier to adoption wasn't the proving, it was getting engineers to write formal specs at all. Models are good at translating between natural language, code, and formal logic, so they can help draft a spec from a design doc or from a comment, and then a human can review it. The other is the volume of proof engineering. A big proof of a cryptographic library or a hypervisor has thousands of small lemmas, most of them tedious. If a model can knock out eighty percent of those, the human experts can spend their time on the parts that actually require insight.

And the flip side is that verification is one of the most promising tools we have for making generative AI trustworthy. If I can take code that a model wrote and prove it correct against a spec, I don't need to care how the code was produced. So I see the two fields as having a very natural symbiosis right now: AI makes verification cheaper, and verification makes AI's output something you can actually rely on.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting opportunity is to combine the creativity of generative AI with the rigor of automated reasoning. In verification, you often need to come up with something—a specification, an invariant, or a lemma—that makes the proof go through. Finding that can be difficult, even when checking it is relatively straightforward.

Generative AI can propose those candidates. Then a verification tool can check them. If a candidate is wrong, the tool can provide feedback, perhaps a counterexample, and the model can try again. So you have this interaction where the model helps explore possible solutions and the verifier establishes whether they actually work.

That means we don’t need the model to be right every time to be useful. We need it to suggest things that help us make progress, while keeping the proof obligation precise. Of course, we still have to ask whether the specification captures what we intended. But this combination could make verification much more accessible and reduce the expert effort required to apply it.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s exciting to me is that generative AI and program verification have complementary strengths. In verification, we often know how to check a proof once we have it. The hard part is finding the proof—coming up with the right invariant, the right abstraction, or the right intermediate lemma. That requires a kind of creativity, and generative AI gives us a new way to propose those things.

Now, the model can be wrong. But if it proposes an invariant, we can use a verification tool to check whether that invariant actually holds and whether it’s sufficient to establish the property we care about. If it fails, we can feed that information back and try again. So you get this interesting loop between generating candidates and rigorously checking them.

That could make verification accessible to many more people. Today, a lot of the effort requires specialized expertise. If AI can help with that work, while the verification tools provide the mathematical checks, we have a path toward applying verification much more broadly.
